The proposed solution is incorrect. 

A wall consists of horizontal layers of the same total width stacked vertically. In layer $n$, the layer is partitioned into $2^n - 1$ identical rectangular bricks, meaning that each brick in layer $n$ has width $\frac{W}{2^n - 1}$ (where $W$ is the total width of the wall). 

For example, the single brick in layer 1 spans the entire width $[0, W]$, while layer 2 has 3 bricks spanning $[0, W/3]$, $[W/3, 2W/3]$, and $[2W/3, W]$. The brick in layer 1 shares a horizontal boundary segment with all three bricks in layer 2, meaning Jessica already has 3 distinct choices on her very first move. 

The proposed solution incorrectly assumes that every brick across all layers has width 1 (which would make each layer have a different total width) and artificially left-aligns them. Thus, the total number of sequences of moves is strictly greater than 1.

VERDICT: REJECT
